summary: Wayne Hathaway's comments on the new Telnet protocol and option specifications. He thinks they are far better than before but objects to details, especially the notes on option subnegotiation and how Telnet SYNCH is handled when there is more than one Telnet interpreter. RFC 529 replies.

plainLanguage.summary: A reader of the new rules for remote typing praised them but pointed out a few spots that could confuse real programs.

subtitle: A reader praises the new Telnet specifications, then lists the spots he thinks should change.

tldr.problem: The proposed new Telnet protocol and option specifications had unclear spots: how option subnegotiation parameters are parsed, what counts as an "interesting" thing during a synch, and some wording.
tldr.mechanism: Wayne Hathaway proposes delimiting subnegotiation parameters at the end and requiring them to double IAC, narrowing a synch to "discard all input up to and including the next DM command", and several editorial fixes.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of comments, not a standard. RFC 529 replies to it, agreeing with some points and disagreeing with others.

facts.label: Proposed synch rule
facts.value: Discard input up to and including the next DM

sections.title: Overall Verdict
sections.content: Wayne Hathaway comments on the proposed new Telnet Protocol Specification (NIC # 15372) and Telnet Option Specification (NIC 15373). He feels the new protocol is far superior to the previous version, but says a few items of substance should be changed, along with some editorial points.
sections.plainLanguage: He says the new rules are much better than the old ones, but a few things still need fixing.

sections.title: Subnegotiation and Synch
sections.content:
The most significant error, he says, is in the "Note on 'Sub-negotiations'" section of the Option Specification. It says each party is presumed able to parse the parameters, and that a byte with value 255 inside a subnegotiation need not be doubled like the general Telnet IAC. Hathaway argues this wrongly assumes there is only one "Telnet Interpreter". If a user process carries out the subnegotiation, only that process can read the parameters, so the receiving NCP cannot scan past them when a Telnet synch arrives.

His fix: delimit subnegotiation parameters at the end (perhaps with the same SB command) and make them obey all Telnet rules, including doubling IAC. He also objects to the loose definition of "interesting" things and proposes that only the DM command count, so a synch means "discard all input up to and including the next DM command".

To protect option requests that a synch might discard, he floats a "synch response" (SR) command or a TIMING-MARK sent after the DM. A final substantive request is some way to specify horizontal tab positions and use, perhaps as an option.
sections.plainLanguage: When a program is told to skip ahead, the helper skipping ahead has to know where the skipping part ends. He wants every special message to have a clear ending, like a closing bracket.

sections.title: Editorial Comments
sections.content:
The editorial comments refer to the Telnet Protocol document by page. Hathaway asks that the phrase "blocked on input" (page 8) be removed or reworded, that the Abort Output (AO) command (page 10) say when output resumes, and that the "over-strike" example for EC (page 11) be clarified, along with what EC and EL mean on output.

He would drop or define the word "promptly" (page 11), change the line about discarding characters so that BELLs are discarded too (page 12), and add support for, or remove, the rule that CR NUL must generate a CR only (page 14).
sections.plainLanguage: He also lists small wording problems, like a teacher marking confusing sentences in a rulebook.

references.text: Proposed new TELNET Protocol Specification, NIC # 15372.
